en.marketHeading: What is actually different about marketing in {city}
market: {city} sits at the western end of the Greater Toronto and {city} Area, close enough that Toronto advertisers routinely target it and far enough that most of your customers would never drive into Toronto for what you sell. That mismatch is where {city} ad budgets leak. If your targeting is loose, you are bidding in the same auctions as businesses with ten times your budget for clicks that were never going to become customers.

The fix is unglamorous and it is most of the work: geography tightened to the area you actually serve, a negative keyword list that excludes the Toronto-intent searches, and conversion tracking that counts a booked job rather than a form view so you can see which side of the border is actually paying you. Doing that properly is usually worth more to a {city} business than any increase in budget.

Underneath that, {city} has a real economy of its own. Health care and life sciences around the hospital network, advanced manufacturing, logistics along the highway corridor and a construction sector working through years of growth. Those are all markets where local search still decides who gets the call, which is why the geography question matters so much.

faq.q: Do you have an office in {city}?
faq.a: No. I am based in Toronto and work from home, so there is no {city} office and I am not going to imply there is. Everything is run remotely over video and email, which is how I run every account.

faq.q: Should we target Toronto as well?
faq.a: Only if you genuinely serve it and can compete on price there. For most {city} businesses the answer is no, and the more useful move is excluding Toronto properly so your budget stops funding clicks from people who will hire somebody closer to home. If you do serve Toronto, it should be its own campaign with its own budget so you can see whether it pays.

faq.q: Why are our clicks so expensive?
faq.a: Usually because the account is competing in a wider market than the business does. Loose geographic targeting, broad match keywords and a thin negative list all pull you into auctions against advertisers with far bigger budgets. That is fixable and it is normally the first thing I would change.
